conditions.name: Vaginal candidiasis

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

conditions.summary: A very common overgrowth of Candida yeast (normally present in small amounts) causing intense vulval itching, soreness, and a thick, white, curd-like discharge -- NOT primarily sexually transmitted, unlike the other conditions sharing this bundle. Often triggered by recent antibiotics, pregnancy, or poorly-controlled diabetes. Recurrent episodes (4 or more a year) or symptoms not responding to standard treatment deserve proper assessment rather than repeated self-treatment, including a check for underlying diabetes.
workup: Usually a clinical diagnosis on the classic itch + discharge pattern
Over-the-counter or prescription antifungal (topical clotrimazole or oral fluconazole)
Avoid tight synthetic underwear and scented vaginal products, which can worsen irritation
Check blood glucose if episodes are recurrent -- poorly-controlled diabetes is a real, treatable trigger
Specialist referral for recurrent (4+ episodes/year) or treatment-resistant cases

exam.step: Ask specifically whether the discharge itches or is just noticed as an odour/appearance change
exam.positive: BV is classically NOT itchy -- a genuine distinguishing feature from candidiasis, the closest differential sharing this bundle

exam.step: Ask about a fishy odour, especially noticeable after sex
exam.positive: A characteristic, near-diagnostic feature of BV

exam.step: Inspect for a thin, greyish-white discharge coating the vaginal walls
exam.positive: The classic appearance, distinct from candidiasis's thick white discharge

labs.test: Clinical diagnosis (Amsel criteria) or vaginal pH testing
labs.confirms: Elevated vaginal pH (above 4.5) supports the diagnosis alongside the characteristic discharge and odour

labs.test: Vaginal swab microscopy (Gram stain, Nugent score)
labs.confirms: The laboratory gold standard when the diagnosis is uncertain

conditions.name: Bacterial vaginosis

triage.label: See a doctor soon
triage.action: Arrange an appointment in the next day or two

conditions.summary: An imbalance of normal vaginal bacteria producing a thin, greyish-white discharge with a characteristic fishy odour, often more noticeable after sex -- classically NOT itchy or sore, a genuine distinguishing feature from candidiasis. Not strictly classed as a sexually transmitted infection, though it is linked to sexual activity. Worth treating properly (not just masking the odour) since untreated BV genuinely raises the risk of pelvic infection and complications in pregnancy.
workup: Usually a clinical diagnosis on the discharge character and odour, sometimes supported by vaginal pH testing
Oral or vaginal metronidazole -- the standard, effective treatment
Avoid vaginal douching, which disrupts normal flora and can worsen or trigger BV
Treatment in pregnancy is genuinely important -- untreated BV is linked to preterm birth risk, so don't just tolerate the odour

exam.step: Inspect for a frothy, yellow-green, malodorous discharge
exam.positive: The classic appearance, distinct from candidiasis (white, curd-like) and BV (thin, greyish)

exam.step: Ask about a new or non-monogamous sexual partner, or a partner with symptoms
exam.positive: Trichomoniasis is a genuine STI -- unlike candidiasis/BV, sexual history is a real, relevant risk factor here

exam.step: Ask specifically about partner treatment when giving results/advice
exam.positive: Untreated partners lead to reinfection -- a genuinely important, sometimes overlooked management point

labs.confirms: The most sensitive test, now the standard confirmatory investigation

conditions.name: Trichomoniasis

triage.label: See a doctor soon
triage.action: Arrange an appointment in the next day or two

conditions.summary: A genuine sexually transmitted infection caused by the protozoan parasite Trichomonas vaginalis -- classically a frothy, yellow-green, malodorous discharge with vulval irritation and dysuria, though a substantial proportion of infections are mild or asymptomatic. Unlike candidiasis and bacterial vaginosis, this genuinely needs treating the sexual partner(s) too, or reinfection is very likely -- an important point patients are not always told.
workup: Vaginal swab NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test) -- the most sensitive confirmatory test
Oral metronidazole (single dose or a 7-day course, per current guidance) -- the standard, effective treatment
Treat sexual partner(s) at the same time, and avoid sex until both are treated and symptoms have resolved -- otherwise reinfection is very likely
Screen for other STIs, since co-infection is common

exam.step: Ask about dysuria, discharge (penile or vaginal), and any pelvic/testicular discomfort
exam.positive: The classic urethritis/cervicitis pattern, though genuinely often mild or absent -- a normal exam does not exclude infection

exam.step: Take a sexual history -- new/multiple partners, condom use, partner symptoms
exam.positive: The single most important risk-factor question for this condition specifically

exam.step: In women, examine for cervicitis (inflamed, friable cervix, mucopurulent discharge); in men, for urethral discharge
exam.positive: Supportive findings, though testing (not examination alone) confirms the diagnosis

labs.confirms: The standard, highly sensitive test for both organisms
Allows antibiotic susceptibility testing, important given rising resistance concerns

conditions.name: Gonorrhoea / Chlamydia

triage.label: See a doctor soon
triage.action: Arrange an appointment in the next day or two

conditions.summary: The two most common bacterial sexually transmitted infections -- causing urethritis/cervicitis with dysuria and discharge, though a genuinely large proportion of infections (especially chlamydia) are mild or entirely asymptomatic, which is exactly why they spread so easily and why opportunistic screening matters. Affects men and women. Left untreated, both can cause serious complications -- pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility risk in women, epididymitis in men -- so prompt treatment and partner notification genuinely matter, not just symptom relief.
workup: NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test) on a urine sample or swab -- the standard test for both infections
Ceftriaxone (single injection) for gonorrhoea, doxycycline (7-day course) for chlamydia, per current guidance -- treatment differs by organism, so testing before treating matters
Partner notification and treatment -- essential to prevent reinfection and interrupt onward spread
Screen for other STIs, since co-infection is common
Avoid sex until treatment is completed and partner(s) have also been treated

exam.step: Inspect the glans and foreskin for redness, swelling, discharge, and whether the foreskin can be retracted
exam.positive: The genuine hallmark findings -- not directly captured by a dedicated node in this checker, an important disclosed limitation

exam.step: Ask about diabetes symptoms or check blood glucose, particularly for recurrent or non-responding cases
exam.positive: Recurrent candidal balanitis is a genuine, well-documented presenting feature of previously undiagnosed diabetes

exam.step: Ask specifically about fever or feeling generally unwell, looking for their ABSENCE
exam.positive: Balanitis/phimosis is usually a localised, mild condition -- systemic symptoms should prompt considering a more serious cause instead

labs.test: Clinical examination of the glans and foreskin
labs.confirms: Usually sufficient for diagnosis

labs.test: Blood glucose / HbA1c if recurrent or not responding to standard treatment
labs.confirms: Screens for underlying undiagnosed diabetes

conditions.name: Balanitis / phimosis

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

conditions.summary: Inflammation of the glans penis and/or foreskin (balanitis), often with an inability to retract a tight foreskin (phimosis) -- the two are grouped together here since they commonly occur together and predispose to each other. DISCLOSED PROXY LIMITATION: no evidence node in this catalogue captures genital redness, soreness or discharge directly -- this condition is modelled through the closest available proxies (soreness passing urine through inflamed tissue, and generic itching), not a perfect match for its actual presenting features.
workup: Ask about foreskin retractability, redness/swelling of the glans, discharge under the foreskin, and hygiene practices
Screen for undiagnosed diabetes, particularly with recurrent or candidal-pattern balanitis -- a genuine, well-documented association
Topical antifungal (if candidal) or mild topical steroid cream, plus improved hygiene, for most straightforward cases
Referral for circumcision or preputioplasty if phimosis is persistent, causing recurrent balanitis, or causing obstructed urination

exam.step: Ask specifically about pelvic, perineal or lower back pain, not just urinary symptoms
exam.positive: The genuine hallmark distinguishing this from BPH, which does not typically cause significant pain

exam.step: Ask about fever and systemic illness, looking for their presence in ACUTE cases and absence in CHRONIC cases
exam.positive: Fever suggests acute bacterial prostatitis needing prompt antibiotics; its absence with a long duration fits the far more common chronic CP/CPPS pattern

exam.step: Ask about age and the pace of onset
exam.positive: Prostatitis genuinely skews younger/middle-aged and can have a more acute onset, unlike BPH's older-skewed, gradual, progressive course

labs.confirms: Identifies a bacterial cause where present, though many chronic CP/CPPS cases have no identifiable infection
An exquisitely tender, boggy prostate supports acute bacterial prostatitis

labs.test: PSA (interpreted with caution -- can be modestly raised by prostatitis itself, not just prostate pathology)
labs.confirms: Should not be relied on alone during an active flare

conditions.name: Prostatitis (acute / chronic pelvic pain syndrome)

triage.label: See a doctor soon
triage.action: Arrange an appointment in the next day or two

conditions.summary: Inflammation of the prostate gland, ranging from acute bacterial prostatitis (sudden onset, often with fever) to chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome (CP/CPPS, the far more common form -- persistent pelvic/perineal pain and urinary symptoms lasting months, often without a proven infection). Distinct from Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) sharing this bundle: prostatitis genuinely skews younger/middle-aged with a more prominent pain component, rather than BPH's older-skewed, slowly progressive voiding-symptom picture.
workup: Ask specifically about pelvic, perineal, or lower back pain alongside urinary symptoms -- the genuine hallmark distinguishing this from simple voiding-symptom conditions like BPH
Urine culture and, for acute presentations, blood tests/cultures if systemically unwell -- to identify or exclude acute bacterial prostatitis
Antibiotics for confirmed or suspected bacterial prostatitis (acute cases genuinely need prompt antibiotic treatment)
Alpha-blockers, pelvic floor physiotherapy, and a multimodal approach (pain management, lifestyle measures) for chronic CP/CPPS, per current AUA guidance
Digital rectal examination -- helps distinguish acute bacterial prostatitis (an exquisitely tender, boggy prostate) from other causes, though should be done gently

redFlags.label: Possible sepsis
redFlags.message: A fever together with confusion, very fast breathing, mottled skin or a collapsing blood pressure can mean infection is affecting the whole body.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now. Do not wait to see whether it settles.

redFlags.label: Rash that does not fade under pressure
redFlags.message: Spots that stay visible when a glass is pressed on them, alongside feeling unwell, can be a sign of bacteria in the bloodstream.

redFlags.label: Possible severe allergic reaction
redFlags.message: Swelling of the throat or tongue with difficulty breathing after a food, sting, or medicine can close the airway within minutes.
redFlags.action: Use an adrenaline auto-injector if you have one, then call emergency services.

redFlags.label: Reduced consciousness
redFlags.message: Being difficult to rouse, or drifting in and out of awareness, always needs immediate assessment whatever the cause.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now. Place the person on their side if unresponsive.

redFlags.label: Possible stroke
redFlags.message: Sudden facial drooping, arm weakness or difficulty speaking is a stroke until proven otherwise. Treatment works only within a few hours.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now and note the exact time symptoms began.

redFlags.label: Seizure
redFlags.message: A first seizure needs assessment to find the cause and to advise on driving and safety.
redFlags.action: Seek urgent assessment today. Call emergency services if the seizure lasted over five minutes or a second one followed.

redFlags.label: Significant gastrointestinal bleeding
redFlags.message: Vomiting blood, or passing black tarry stools, means bleeding inside the digestive tract.
redFlags.action: Go to an emergency department now.

redFlags.label: Pelvic pain with a missed period
redFlags.message: One-sided pelvic pain with a late or missed period can mean a pregnancy growing outside the womb, which can bleed suddenly and heavily.
redFlags.action: Take a pregnancy test and go to an emergency department or early pregnancy unit today.

redFlags.label: Sudden severe testicular pain
redFlags.message: A testicle that becomes suddenly and severely painful may have twisted and lost its blood supply. It can only be saved within a few hours.
redFlags.action: Go to an emergency department now. Do not eat or drink.

redFlags.label: New jaundice
redFlags.message: Yellowing of the skin or eyes always needs blood tests to find out why.

redFlags.label: Sudden loss of vision
redFlags.message: Sight lost suddenly in one or both eyes needs assessment the same hour, whatever the cause.
redFlags.action: Go to an eye emergency department now.

redFlags.label: Thoughts of self-harm
redFlags.message: Thoughts of harming yourself or of being better off dead deserve help today. You do not have to be in crisis to reach out.
redFlags.action: Contact your doctor, a crisis line, or go to an emergency department now. If you are in immediate danger, call emergency services.

redFlags.label: New confusion coming on over hours or days
redFlags.message: Confusion that has come on over hours or days, or that comes and goes through the day, is delirium until proven otherwise. It is caused by something else -- an infection, a drug, pain, retention -- and that cause needs finding today.
redFlags.action: Seek same-day medical assessment. Take a list of all medications. Call emergency services if they are drowsy, feverish or cannot be roused properly.

disclaimer: This tool provides information about possible causes of symptoms. It is not a diagnosis and it cannot examine you. It does not replace assessment by a qualified clinician. If you feel very unwell, or your symptoms are getting rapidly worse, seek medical help immediately regardless of what this tool says.
